abstract: In automobile markets where consumers attach social recognition to car ownership, how does the introduction of a lower‐cost alternative influence the market outcomes of traditional internal combustion engine vehicles (ICEVs)? Leveraging high‐frequency sales data covering China's entire automobile market from 2018 to 2022, we examine heterogeneous market responses to the emergence of electric vehicles (EVs) across different price segments. Overall, the rise of EVs is associated with lower ICEV sales but higher total automobile sales. More importantly, while EV penetration is negatively correlated with ICEV sales in the low‐ and mid‐end segments, it is positively correlated with ICEV sales in the high‐end segment. Further evidence suggests that the rise of EVs amplifies the symbolic value of high‐end ICEVs, boosting sales of ICEV models with strong social recognition.

title: A car for recognition: The heterogeneous market responses to the emergence of electric vehicles

abstract: We study platform growth in a field experiment with drivers on a peer‐to‐peer carpooling platform in Singapore. Motivated by both theory and observed practice, we ask whether temporary subsidies and informational campaigns can have durable effects on the growth of platforms. Drivers were randomly assigned to different standard promotional strategies: some drivers receive information about favorable market conditions, others receive subsidies for picking up passengers. Informational nudges re‐engage dormant drivers in the short run, but the effect is temporary and does not generate durable market growth. While subsidies may generate a small initial increase in participation, they reduce participation in the longer term. Estimating drivers' preferences, we find that drivers may adjust their selectivity when they know they are scarce relative to passengers—an equilibrium response in matching markets that explains why, in settings with multidimensional preferences, standard promotional strategies may fail to generate durable growth.
title: Platform Growth Is Hard: Experimental and Quasi‐Experimental Evidence From a Carpooling Platform in Singapore

abstract: Many developing countries engage in policy experimentation to mitigate the uncertainty associated with reform. Although it is widely acknowledged in academia that pilot-type environmental policies (PEP) can reduce trial-and-error costs, their institutional characteristics and potential challenges remain under-explored. Taking the Air Pollution Joint Prevention and Control Policy (APJPCP) in Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei (BTH) and neighboring regions as a case study, we evaluate PEP's value and challenges by combining a two-party evolutionary game (TEG) model with a Difference-in-Differences (DID) approach. Based on confirming the policy's overall effectiveness, we identify a structural imbalance across pilot batches: the promotion group significantly outperforms the pilot group. On the one hand, Rational Policy Expectations (RPE) enable late-movers to leverage verified information to enhance policy efficiency. On the other hand, the surge in cross-batch coordination costs makes first-movers more prone to falling into the governance dilemma under the Institutional Collective Action (ICA) framework, thereby inducing governance distortions and strategic responses from micro-agents. Taken together, while environmental policy experiments possess indispensable institutional value in theory, the complexity of their implementation process poses challenges to the institutional transition of developing countries.

abstract: This paper studies how expected inflation affects the timing of corporate investment when cash flows adjust sluggishly and liabilities are nominal. Two mechanisms operate: expected inflation delays investment by reducing the real value of future cash flows and raising discount rates, while inflation erodes the real burden of nominal debt and mitigates Myers-type overhang, especially when maturities are long. Using firm-quarter hazards of investment spikes from 1972 to 2023, a 1-percentage-point increase in expected inflation is associated with a reduction in the quarterly hazard of investing of roughly one third, an association concentrated in periods of high expected inflation. The mitigating effect is strongest for firms with high leverage and long-maturity debt structures, in line with the model's comparative statics.
title: Inflation, debt overhang and corporate investment

abstract: While decarbonizing China's energy-intensive industries is critical for achieving the dual carbon goals, existing research lacks a unified framework to reconcile the contradictory pressures between institutional race-to-the-bottom (RTB) effects induced by local government competition and emission reduction dividends from supply chain synergy. Grounded in the promotion tournament system, this study develops an institutional competition and market synergy analytical framework. Using provincial-industry panel data, this study employs System GMM, IV-2SLS, and continuous staggered DID estimations to examine the environmental effects of spatial linkages and their institutional reshaping mechanisms in energy-intensive industries. Empirical findings demonstrate that, first, driven by inter-governmental competition, specialized spatial proximity significantly exacerbates carbon emission intensity, confirming the institutional RTB hypothesis. Second, vertically-linked spatial proximity exhibits asymmetric market dynamics. Upstream supply proximity substantially reduces emissions via supply chain synergy, whereas administrative market segmentation impedes the emission-reduction dividends of downstream market proximity. Third, the environmental impact of local agglomeration follows a conditional U-shaped relationship moderated by local externality structures rather than a deterministic inverted U-shaped trajectory. Fourth, quasi-natural experiment evidence from the Central Environmental Protection Inspection confirms that top-down exogenous institutional constraints effectively correct local governments' performance incentives and significantly mitigate the emission-increasing effects of the institutional RTB. This study elucidates the spatial evolutionary mechanisms of carbon emissions under the dual constraints of institutional games and market forces, offering targeted insights for optimizing regional industrial spatial governance.

title: Institutional race-to-the-bottom and asymmetric market synergy: Spatial linkages and carbon emissions in China's energy-intensive industries

abstract: We study a decreasing price auction with an ambiguity-neutral seller and two ambiguity-averse buyers. Due to the dynamic structure, buyers learn about the valuation of the opponent buyer during the auction. We characterize a belief-formation process that allows buyers to consider their knowledge of the information structure. This process leads to a rectangular ex-ante belief set and implies dynamically consistent behavior. We show that, in this setting, rectangularity and consistent planning can yield different equilibrium outcomes. Under rectangularity, buyers are even more pessimistic and may therefore be willing to accept higher prices. Thus, for a fixed auction mechanism, the seller can extract a higher surplus. Furthermore, we show that the seller can extract almost all surplus even if buyers behave dynamically consistently.
title: Dynamic Consistency in Ambiguous Dutch Auctions

abstract: A common assumption in climate and development policy is that shifting activity toward services makes growth cleaner. We test it on an unbalanced panel of 147 countries over 1991–2021, using the World Bank’s monetised CO2 damage series, the quantity to which a social-cost-of-carbon schedule is applied, as the outcome. Services expansion is associated with higher, not lower, monetised damage. Within countries, conditional on the other sectors and the energy controls, a one-dollar larger annual increase in services value added accompanies a 1.38-cent larger increase in damage. The elasticity is 0.25 in log-differences. The association is smallest, and imprecisely estimated, in low-income economies, significantly below every other group under a country-level bootstrap, and lies between one and two cents per dollar in the other groups. In proportional terms the ordering reverses, the elasticity rising with income. The association is stronger where fossil-electricity dependence and energy demand are rising, and it is unchanged when the relative price of services is controlled for, which weighs against a Baumol cost-disease artefact. It survives GDP weighting, alternative estimators, region-by-year fixed effects and permutation placebos. Because the social cost of carbon multiplies an emissions base and is itself a marginal-damage concept, the composition of growth enters that base rather than the price per tonne. Read as a baseline, the estimated intensities show that a uniform-composition projection understates the emissions base of middle-income economies expanding services on fossil-energy systems, while leaving the global total little changed. Emissions baselines for social-cost-of-carbon calibration should therefore be structure-aware.
title: The carbon damage of services-led growth: Structure-aware baselines for the social cost of carbon

abstract: Studies of California's $20 fast-food minimum wage disagree about whether it reduced employment. Much of the disagreement arises from a substantial number of seemingly innocuous researcher decisions on comparison group construction. This column reports the results of 1,440 plausible synthetic-control specifications. More than 96% of the estimates show job losses, but the range is wide. Estimates that imply no effect sit in the tail of the distribution. By contrast, the estimates that arise from simple comparisons between California and the rest of the US imply an employment decline of around 3% and land near the distribution’s centre. The authors argue that results should be shown across a range of defensible choices.
authors: Jeffrey Clemens, Olivia Edwards, Jonathan Meer, Joshua Nguyen
title: Researcher choices matter: Synthetic controls and California’s $20 fast-food minimum wage
